rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: In the HCP-D dataset, T1w structural MRI data were bias-field-corrected and skull stripped, following which the cortical surfaces were reconstructed. Structural images were segmented into the cerebrospinal fluid, gray matter, and white matter, and then spatially normalized to the standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space. Blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) time-series data underwent slice-timing correction, rigid-body transformation-based motion correction, intensity inhomogeneity correction, co-registration with structural images, normalization to the MNI space, and projection onto the cortical surface [28]. Surface-based spatial smoothing with a 2 mm full width at half maximum (FWHM) was subsequently performed. A bandpass filter (0.008-0.1 Hz) was then applied, and six head motion parameters were regressed out.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Centile scores; Functional hierarchy score (cosine similarity between individual gradient and normative gradient)
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper uses two main deviation metrics: (1) Centile scores, which quantify age- and sex-specific deviations in gradient values across developmental stages by comparing individual features to the normative distribution; (2) Functional hierarchy score, computed as the cosine similarity between an individual's gradient and the normative gradient for their age, serving as a whole-brain summary metric.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: To quantify the extent to which an individual deviates from normative trajectories, we calculated centile scores, which serve as age- and sex-specific indicators of deviations in gradient values across developmental stages. The centile score was determined by comparing each individual's brain features (i.e., gradient value) with those from the normative distribution... We devised a functional hierarchy score as a summary metric (i.e., a scalar value for the whole brain), representing the relative closeness of individual data points with respect to the normative cortical functional hierarchy. We defined this as the cosine similarity between an individual's gradient (G1) and the normative gradient for their age (NormG1age), as estimated by the GAMLSS model.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Two-sample t-tests comparing centile scores between ASD and TD groups with FDR correction for multiple comparisons across brain regions; Linear models controlling for age and sex to compare gradient values between groups (implemented in BrainStat toolbox); Age-bin analysis dividing participants into three developmental stages (childhood 5-12 years, early adolescence 12-15 years, adolescence/young adults 15-22 years) with network-level stratification and statistical testing; Pearson correlation analysis between hierarchy scores and Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS) total and subscores (awareness, cognition, communication, motivation, mannerisms); Mediation analysis using bootstrap (5,000 iterations) to examine whether whole-brain and network-specific participation coefficient (PC) centile scores mediated the relationship between diagnostic group and hierarchy score, implemented using lavaan R package; Analysis of variance (sigma) in GAMLSS model to assess heterogeneity across age; Spatial correlation analyses for sensitivity analyses comparing different parcellation schemes and thresholds
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Individuals with ASD showed a nonlinear developmental trajectory of cortical hierarchy with delayed maturation in childhood, accelerated catch-up during adolescence, and subsequent decline in young adulthood, with persistent DMN dysfunction throughout development being a key contributor mediated by reduced network segregation.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study found that cortical hierarchy maturation in ASD followed a distinct nonlinear trajectory compared to TD individuals. During childhood (5-12 years), ASD individuals showed pronounced deviations in both sensory networks (somatomotor t=3.43 p=0.001, dorsal attention t=4.78 p<1e-4, ventral attention t=4.27 p<1e-4) and DMN (t=-5.67 p<1e-6), with hierarchy scores showing a steeper increase (slope 0.013/year) compared to TD (slope 0.009/year for males). The ASD group caught up to typical cortical hierarchy around age 14.78 years for males and 14.98 years for females, followed by a decline. In early adolescence (12-15 years), network-level significance diminished except for somatomotor (t=2.62 p=0.035) and DMN (t=-2.86 p=0.035). In late adolescence and young adulthood (15-22 years), deviations were predominantly driven by decreased gradient values in DMN precuneus and posterior cingulate cortex (t=-3.72 p=0.002) and increased values in control network (t=2.88 p=0.016). Mediation analyses revealed that reduced DMN segregation was the only significant mediator of reduced hierarchy scores in adolescence and young adulthood. Hierarchy scores significantly correlated with SRS total and all five subscores (average r=-0.118), with the highest correlation in the communication subdomain, indicating lower hierarchy scores (greater deviation) associated with higher symptom severity. The TD group showed decreasing variance (sigma) with age (t=-2.415 p=0.016), indicating convergence to norms, while ASD showed no change (t=0.047 p=0.96), suggesting persistent heterogeneity. Findings were replicated in ABIDE-II and validated in a longitudinal subset.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Small sample size particularly in older age range limiting generalizability; Uneven age distribution across developmental stages; Uncertainty in trajectories at age extremes; Limited longitudinal data with small sample sizes and short follow-up intervals; Potential overfitting and complexity in GAMLSS interpretation; Cross-sectional design limits causal inference
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Despite its strengths, this study has several limitations. First, the small sample size, particularly in participants in the older age range, limited the generalizability of our findings, especially regarding the developmental trajectory during late adolescence and young adulthood. Uncertainty in the trajectory significantly increased at age extremes where data points are limited, making it difficult to draw robust conclusions regarding these developmental periods [72]. The linear trajectories observed in the replication dataset (i.e., ABIDE-II) likely arose from age distribution imbalances... Although our longitudinal analysis supports the interpretation of age-related associations as developmental trajectories, it is important to acknowledge certain caveats. Longitudinal datasets remain limited in ASD research, and factors such as small sample sizes, short follow-up intervals, and demographic heterogeneity may influence the generalizability of these results... The use of GAMLSS for modeling nonlinear trajectories also faces inherent challenges, such as potential overfitting and complexity in interpretation, which could affect the robustness of the results [43].

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study used three developmental stage bins following prior research classifications (childhood 5-12, early adolescence 12-15, adolescence/young adults 15-22 years). Transfer learning approach was employed when applying HCP-D normative model to ABIDE datasets, with intercept re-estimation while preserving nonlinear age effects. The functional hierarchy score provides a whole-brain scalar summary metric with potential clinical utility for identifying critical developmental windows for intervention. Sensitivity analyses included uniform age resampling (100 iterations) for ABIDE-II to address age distribution imbalance, demonstrating retention of nonlinear trajectory patterns. The study also examined second gradient (sensorimotor-visual axis) showing similar but weaker patterns than the primary gradient.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The paper notes a discrepancy between the stated total N=652 for HCP-D and the sum of reported sex counts (301M + 251F = 552); this discrepancy should be noted. The study employed both ABIDE-I (discovery) and ABIDE-II (replication) datasets, with additional validation using ABIDE-II longitudinal subset (n=38). The normative model used SHASH distribution recommended for neuroimaging normative modeling. ComBat harmonization was applied after gradient estimation and Procrustes alignment. The study examined both the first gradient (sensory-DMN axis, primary focus) and second gradient (sensorimotor-visual axis, supplementary). Participation coefficient was used as a measure of network integration/segregation. Age range for all analyses was 5-22 years. SRS behavioral data were available for ABIDE-I (n=240) and ABIDE-II (n=538) subsets, with subdomain scores only available for ABIDE-II. The study used a 10% connectivity threshold for gradient computation with sensitivity analyses at 5% and 20%.
